item.title: Enhancing analytical photon transport in turbid media through physics-guided neural network corrections
item.description: arXiv:2610.26917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analytical methods provide rapid and computationally efficient predictions of light transport in turbid media, making them attractive for real-time and inverse applications. However, their accuracy is limited by the approximations and assumptions used to obtain tractable solutions. On the other hand, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is widely regarded as the "gold standard" for modeling light transport in turbid media, but its high computational cost limits its use in applications requiring repeated forward evaluations. Here, we introduce a physics-guided residual learning framework that combines the computational efficiency of analytical modeling with the accuracy of MC simulation. As a representative case study, we consider the diffusion approximation (DA), which can exhibit systematic errors under relatively strong absorption, weak scattering, and imperfect boundary treatment. Given the absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, and anisotropy factor, the corresponding DA prediction is incorporated as a physical prior, while the network learns only the residual between the analytical prediction and the MC reference. Across the evaluated optical-property range, the proposed framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of approximately 62 and 14, respectively, relative to the diffusion approximation. With only 1\% of the available training data, it achieves approximately 87\% and 93\% lower corresponding errors than a direct neural-network surrogate. These results demonstrate that learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Guojun Tang, Paul D. Teal, Alexander Doronin

item.title: Gerchberg-Saxton Optimized Silicon Metasurface for Sinusoidal Structured-Light Three-Dimensional Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.26956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) optical imaging based on structured illumination has attracted considerable attention in applications including machine vision, robotics, and computational sensing. However, conventional structured-light systems generally rely on bulky projection components, such as digital micromirror devices and diffractive optical elements, which limit system miniaturization and integration. Here, we demonstrate a compact structured-light 3D imaging platform enabled by a silicon dielectric metasurface operating at a near-infrared wavelength of 940 nm. The desired sinusoidal fringe illumination is encoded into the metasurface through a Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) phase optimization algorithm, which converts the target far-field distribution into a nanoscale phase profile and subsequently into silicon nanopillar geometries. The fabricated metasurface generates high-quality sinusoidal structured illumination, which is integrated with a four-step phase-shifting reconstruction method to recover 3D object profiles. The proposed approach provides a compact and scalable solution for miniaturized structured-light projection and optical 3D sensing.
item.dc:creator: Gengyuan Ye, Shuming Wang

item.title: Shaping the spectra of second harmonic laser by spatial focusing
item.description: arXiv:2610.27011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurately controlling the spectral width of second harmonic generation (SHG) is critical in applications such as nonlinear microscopy, ultrafast spectroscopy, and quantum optics, where tailored spectral properties are required. Although it is known that the focal length of the lens used to focus the pump beam influences the SHG spectrum, a simple and precise theoretical understanding of this effect has been lacking. Here, we develop a theoretical model to describe how pump focusing conditions affect SHG spectral broadening, and experimentally validate the model using BBO crystals with lenses of 50 mm and 200 mm focal lengths. Our results establish a practical method for engineering the SHG spectral width through pump focusing, providing valuable guidance for designing nonlinear optical systems with specific spectral requirements.
item.dc:creator: Yan-Ming Liu, Tao Xie, Xiangying Hao, Rui-Bo Jin

item.title: Allight: A Perfect Photon Collector
item.description: arXiv:2610.27161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collecting photons from quantum emitters remains a key limitation in light-matter interaction because conventional lenses collect light only from one direction. Here, we introduce a perfect light collector by inverse-designing a surrounding dielectric structure that encloses the emitter to increase photon-collection efficiency toward unity. Decomposing the device into several refractive interfaces enables emission collection from the full 4$\pi$ solid angle with adiabatic reshaping into a collimated beam. We experimentally demonstrate, in two dimensions, the ray bending that collimates omnidirectional emission. Our collector transforms current paradigms for highly efficient photon collection from narrowband, cavity-based techniques into experimentally robust, broadband, non-resonant dielectric devices.
item.dc:creator: Dan Porat, Ran Finkelstein, Tal Carmon

item.title: Controlling Optical Quantum Interference with Plasmonic Metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.27226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to efficiently control optical quantum interference by the same device is a challenging task that promises to enable key operations in quantum information processing. Here, we tackle this problem by presenting a composite quantum plasmonic metasurface operating as an ultrathin non-unitary beamsplitter capable of achieving both single photon bosonic bunching and fermionic anti-bunching interference just by varying the incident photons frequency or changing the design dimensions. The presented metasurface combines a plasmonic grating corrugated by periodic nanoslits that can achieve extraordinary optical transmission with additional nanostripes on top forming nanocavities characterized by localized gap plasmon resonances. The photon-photon interactions are analyzed based on calculating the quantum coalescence metric which accurately portrays the obtained bunching or anti-bunching quantum interference. The presented quantum interference operation is applicable to both fundamental non-classical light interactions and in the design of more applied quantum optical logic gates used in quantum computing and communications.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence M. Qin, Sky Semone, Matthew J. Brandsema, Christos Argyropoulos

item.title: The optical force on a dielectric slab
item.description: arXiv:2610.27254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radiation-pressure forces on transmissive optics, including dynamical backaction, are usually computed from the momentum flux of the external fields. For a dielectric of finite thickness, this omits the time dependence of the electromagnetic momentum stored inside. We compute the force on a lossless dielectric slab of arbitrary thickness $L_s$ submerged in a dielectric fluid, proceeding from both Lorentz force on its bound charges and from the external momentum fluxes for arbitrary carrier and sideband fields. We treat the surrounding medium through a prescribed linear dielectric response and do not model the accompanying mechanical response of the fluid, including pressure and electrostriction. These two methods both recover the expected force in the limit of a thin reflector, but differ in the more general case by the rate of change of the field momentum stored in the slab. This storage term vanishes for static fields and at low frequencies reduces to $(L_s/c^2)\,dP/dt$, where $P$ is the net power through the slab. In a cavity, where $P$ depends on the slab position, the storage term produces a velocity-dependent force. The Abraham and Minkowski momentum formulations applied to the storage term are reconciled to give an unambiguous force on the dielectric in the case of an exterior vacuum environment, where there is no fluid response to model.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Laeuger, Kevin Kuns, Yanbei Chen, Nancy Aggarwal

item.title: Nanophotonic Extreme Ultraviolet Polarimeter
item.description: arXiv:2610.27705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanophotonic engineering has revolutionized how we manipulate the polarization of visible light. Here, we extend such control to extreme ultraviolet radiation, the spectral region of attosecond science and semiconductor lithography, where transmissive optical elements are lacking. We implement channel waveguides that restrict incident 41-nm-wavelength light to a few modes with defined spatial profiles and propagation constants. By designing the propagation-length-dependent interference of two eigenmodes, we achieve polarization-dependent forward scattering, which we exploit to create a transmissive nanophotonic analyzer that resolves the polarization axis and spectrum of extreme ultraviolet light from a single measurement. With a 0.9{\deg}-sensitivity for polarization rotations in a 1-second measurement and single-shot capability, the device opens new experimental opportunities in ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy and at accelerator-based light sources.
item.dc:creator: Anna Kulter, Lorenz Wei{\ss}, David J. Grafinger, Alexander Sagar Grossek, Rodolfo Previdi, Martin Schultze, Marcus Ossiander

item.title: From random patterns to nanophotonic structures: Electromagnetic field prediction without retraining
item.description: arXiv:2610.27769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic surrogate solvers can accelerate nanophotonic design, but their broader use requires accurate predictions for unseen geometries and material arrangements. Training on random dielectric patterns enables direct prediction of complex electromagnetic fields in diverse two-dimensional nanophotonic structures without retraining. The network takes spatial permittivity distributions as inputs, with training samples drawn from a dataset comprising 700,140 combinations of 5,001 random freeform dielectric patterns and 140 relative permittivities from 2.1 to 16.0. The trained model predicts fields for aperiodic bar arrays, manually defined patterns, inverse-designed metalenses, inverse-designed binary structures, and two-material freeform patterns excluded from training. Across 35,441 geometry-permittivity samples, a dilated residual network achieves average relative field errors of 1.4%-7.6%. For 6,950 inverse-designed metalens samples, the three most accurate architectures predict transmitted power with median relative errors of 0.7%-0.9%. Accuracy depends on refractive index and structural scale, with greater errors for patterns coarser than those used for training. These results demonstrate transfer to independently constructed geometries and to new spatial arrangements of dielectric values not represented in the training. Random-pattern training therefore supports reuse of electromagnetic surrogates across multiple structural families, providing a basis for sharing training costs among material screening, iterative optical design, and fabrication-tolerance analysis.
item.dc:creator: Jiwoo Kim, Mingyu Park, Chanik Kang, Hyewon Suk, Haejun Chung

item.title: Controlling exceptional points of layered non-Hermitian structures with magnetic field
item.description: arXiv:2610.27902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional points are the characteristic features of non-Hermitian systems providing numerous applications in optics, acoustics, electronics, etc. We show that exceptional points can be controlled with the external magnetic field by considering the archetypal three-layered $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric photonic structure including a magneto-optic material between the loss and gain layers. Application of the magnetic field makes the system anisotropic with the polarization-sensitive reflection and transmission properties. As a result, the magnetic field can stimulate $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking and mode exchange at realistic values of system parameters. Moreover, we suggest that the proposed scheme can be also used for magnetic-perturbation sensing with an easily adaptable level of desired field strength. Our results contain a valuable evidence for the usefulness of anisotropic (including magnetic) materials for tunable non-Hermitian photonics.
item.dc:creator: Milena Ramanovich, Denis Novitsky

item.title: Enhanced orbital-angular-momentum dimensionality and spatial-spectral decoupling in thin-film SPDC
item.description: arXiv:2610.28020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thin-film spontaneous parametric down-conversion, due to the relaxed phase-matching condition, generates photon pairs that are extremely broadband in frequency and angle and highly entangled in time/frequency and position/momentum. Here we show that it also provides a very broad orbital angular momentum (OAM) spectrum, which, in contrast to the case of bulk crystals, is decoupled from the frequency spectrum. To demonstrate it experimentally, we generate photon pairs in a $7~\mu\mathrm{m}$-thick lithium niobate film and compare them with those from a $500~\mu\mathrm{m}$-thick periodically poled lithium niobate crystal under identical pump conditions. The thin-film source exhibits a substantially broader OAM spectrum, with the azimuthal Schmidt number almost 9 times larger than that of the bulk source. On this highly entangled state, we perform quantum-state tomography in selected two- and four-dimensional OAM subspaces, demonstrating high-purity maximally entangled states. These results highlight thin nonlinear films as a promising platform for high-dimensional quantum-state generation with weak spatial--spectral coupling.
item.dc:creator: Dmitrii Akatev, Jakub Lewandowski, Maria Chekhova

item.title: Attosecond Quantum Optical Spectroscopy of Topological Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.28046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) provides an ultrafast probe of quantum materials, yet conventional spectral observables do not generally furnish a common signature of band topology. Here we show that quantum-light-driven HHG opens an additional information channel through the photon statistics of the emitted harmonics. Using the Haldane Chern insulator and the time-reversal-invariant Kane-Mele topological insulator, we calculate helicity-resolved equal-time intensity correlations and identify a common enhancement of high-order harmonic correlations in the topological phases. For the Haldane model, a dichroic correlation constructed from opposite helicity channels reverses sign with the Chern number. These signatures originate from the distinct nonlinear response sampled by quantum fluctuations of the driving field and are absent from the corresponding mean harmonic spectra as a common classifier. Our results establish photon-correlation spectroscopy as a route to interrogate topological matter with quantum light and provide a bridge between strong-field solid-state physics and quantum optics.
item.dc:creator: C. Granados, J. Rivera-Dean, D. Kim, A. Chac\'on, W. Gao, P. Stammer

item.title: Quantum Limits of Blind Superresolution Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.28089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum estimation has shown that spatial-mode measurements can avoid Rayleigh's curse, but the fundamental precision limits are usually formulated for a known point-spread function (PSF). We show that, for two equally bright incoherent sources sharing an unknown static, shift-invariant complex-amplitude response, the local quantum information for separation is exactly the same as in the known-PSF case. In a quantum semiparametric formulation, the equality follows from the orthogonality of the separation score to the nuisance tangent space generated by all admissible PSF perturbations. We propose two receivers to access this information: momentum-resolved Hong--Ou--Mandel interference (MR-HOM), which acquires half the small-separation quantum information per signal photon without reconstructing the PSF, and a tomography-assisted symmetric logarithmic derivative receiver (TA-SLD), which asymptotically attains the full bound under explicit recovery conditions. These results provide a route toward blind superresolution without prior PSF calibration in microscopy, astronomy, and other optical imaging systems with uncertain responses.
item.dc:creator: Qiushuang Lian, Jun Zhu, Liangcai Cao

item.title: Dual Transverse Vortex-Spin-Momentum Locking in Rotating-Wave Structured Light
item.description: arXiv:2610.28242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically investigate the transverse Poynting momentum and transverse spin angular momentum in circularly polarized rotating-wave structured light, and reveal a pair of \emph{dual} transverse vortex-spin-momentum locking. The transverse Poynting momentum exhibits a $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetric locking structure, being controlled independently by either the polarization or vortex handedness, yet invariant under their simultaneous reversal. Meanwhile, the transverse spin angular momentum is independent of the polarization but endowed with a crucial vortex-dependence inheriting such vortex-dependence from the Poytning momentum via curl operation. This finding expands the understanding of transverse optical linear and angular momenta in structured light and opens a new paradigm for vortex-spin-controlled optical manipulation.
item.dc:creator: Zhen-Lai Wang

item.title: Continuously Tunable Mid-Infrared Metalens Integrating Moir\'e and Pancharatnam-Berry Phases
item.description: arXiv:2610.28389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A varifocal mid-infrared metalens designed for focusing applications is proposed to integrate both Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) and Moir\'e pattern-based mechanisms for rotational wavefront control. The metalens employs two identical nanostructured discs featuring germanium (Ge) meta-atoms on calcium fluoride (CaF2) substrates, operating as birefringent half-wave retarders with 99.95% Polarization Conversion Ratio (PCR) and 83.65% total transmission power at 2 {\mu}m wavelength. Full-wave numerical simulations demonstrate continuous focal length tunability from 45 {\mu}m to 12 {\mu}m by rotating the second disk from 30 deg. to 120 deg., corresponding to the numerical aperture values ranging from 22.99% to 68.67%. The proposed metalens maintains reconfigurable focusing regardless of the incident light polarization, while concurrently enabling polarization-controlled operation via a phase-modulation mechanism that yields inverse responses under Right Circular Polarization (RCP) and Left Circular Polarization (LCP) illuminations.
item.dc:creator: Keivan Kaboutari, Muchuan Chen, Xiu Liu, Sheng Shen, Pedro Pinho, Stanislav Maslovski

item.title: Mechanically reconfigurable layered GRIN lenses for mid-infrared
item.description: arXiv:2610.28398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a concept of mechanically adjustable planar Gradientindex (GRIN) lens that can be used to realize reconfigurable focusing at mid-infrared (mid-IR) or millimeter-wave (mm-wave) frequencies. The concept is based on a multilayer design rooted in effective medium theory, where spatial refractive index profiles are synthesized using first-kind Chebyshev polynomials. Symmetric lateral displacement of the layers enables continuous modulation of the effective refractive index distribution, allowing controlled transitions between divergent, afocal, and convergent wavefronts. Numerical simulations demonstrate accurate focal tuning at mid-IR and mm-waves. In the mid-IR regime, focal lengths of about 56 {\mu}m and 24 {\mu}m are achieved with relative errors of around 4.4% and 10%, respectively. In the mm-wave regime, the lens produces focal lengths of about 158 mm and 128 mm with improved accuracies of 2.3% and 6.0%, respectively. The reconstructed refractive index profiles exhibit high similarity to ideal convex lens distributions, confirming the validity of the proposed synthesis approach. The proposed GRIN lens concept offers a scalable and physically interpretable approach to reconfigurable focusing, with potential applications in multimodal imaging, adaptive sensing, and telecommunication systems.
item.dc:creator: Keivan Kaboutari, Xiu Liu, Sheng Shen, Pedro Pinho, Stanislav Maslovski

item.title: Field demonstration of a self-contained 10 km mobile-to-ground quantum network node via common-aperture co-propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.27427v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we demonstrate a dual-function, common-aperture free-space optical system that simultaneously supports decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) at 803 nm and bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link from a mobile platform to a stationary ground station. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture architecture where a co-propagating classical optical link simultaneously performs full QKD post-processing and ecrypted payload transmission over a 10 km atmospheric channel. The classical link utilizes Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of $\sim$ 0.4 $\%$ (estimated bit error rate (BER) of 3.13 $\times$ 10$^{-5}$) with hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission. Over the 10.31 km link, the QKD system achieved an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 2.512 $\%$ and an average secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Finally, using the distilled keys, real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission was executed over the co-aligned classical optical channel, proving the feasibility of a completely self-contained, jam resistant mobile quantum optical network.
item.dc:creator: Dongkyu Kim, Dong-Gil Im, Kyungdeuk Park, Jisu Kim, Jonguk Choi, Yonggi Jo, Yong Sup Ihn

item.title: Charge-conserving creation and annihilation of topological phase singularities in atomically thin semiconductors
item.description: arXiv:2610.27486v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides provide a promising material platform for optical phase manipulation, as rapid variations in their dielectric functions can give rise to topological phase singularities (PSs). However, PS evolution while preserving topological charge conservation has not yet been investigated in exciton enabled PS systems. Here, using atomically thin MoS2 films on sapphire as a model system, we theoretically and experimentally demonstrate that the evolution of dielectric dispersion determines the creation, trajectory, merging, and annihilation of optical PSs under topological charge conservation. By varying the MoS2 film thickness, we experimentally realize this evolution through the gradual shrinking of the high energy n-k dispersion loop, which modifies its intersection with the zero reflection condition. Our results provide a general strategy for exploring and manipulating topological optical states.
item.dc:creator: Yongjing Wang, Yuhang Wang, Guoshuai Fan, Qingqing Luo, Yanning Li, Lidong Sun, Chunguang Hu, Wanfu Shen

item.title: Single-photon time qubit: Quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time
item.description: arXiv:2610.27639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter is a central challenge in quantum physics. Recently, Bloch~\cite{Bloch2025} proposed the theoretical concept of a \emph{time qubit}, a two-level control space $\mathcal{H}_T=\mathrm{span}\{\ket{+},\ket{-}\}$ that selects between opposite Hamiltonian evolutions $\hat{H}_{\pm}=\hat{H}_0\pm\hat{V}$, but this paradigm has remained experimentally unrealized. Here we formulate the quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit---uncovering quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time---and experimentally probe and validate its predictions using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry from two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources~\cite{Lee2018,Yoon2021}. First, we show theoretically and verify experimentally that a controlled $\pi$ pump--seed phase inversion during pair creation from the quantum vacuum flips the stimulated displacement generator $\hat{V}\to -\hat{V}$ on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background $\hat{H}_0$, reversing the stimulated evolution time [$\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},-}(t)=\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},+}(-t)$] and enabling universal single-qubit $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. Second, we prove that spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch (temporal-direction) information whereas the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams, establishing an exact wave--particle complementarity law $|\bm{r}|=\mathcal{V}=|\alpha|^2/(1+|\alpha|^2)$ for the purity of the arrow of time and enabling direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo.
item.dc:creator: Tai Hyun Yoon

item.title: Narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened multilevel atomic system
item.description: arXiv:2610.27792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We theoretically investigate narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened five-level M-type atomic medium. After Doppler averaging, the M-type system retains a narrow near-resonant electromagnetically induced transparency window that is narrower than that of a standard three-level $\Lambda$ system. This spectral narrowing is associated with the decreasing separation between the two inner dressed states as atomic velocity increases. The transparency window exhibits pronounced direction-dependent transmission, with high forward transmission and strong suppression in the reverse direction. The transparency linewidth and forward-backward probe transmission can be controlled via two independent driving fields, while the central transparency frequency is kept essentially unchanged. The resulting narrowband nonreciprocity supports high forward transmission together with strong suppression in the reverse direction, which is suitable for frequency-selective optical filtering and nonreciprocal optical transmission in thermal atomic media. Our scheme with these specific features is geared towards enabling compact vapor-cell-based nonreciprocal devices for quantum network applications.
item.dc:creator: Ying-Xue Zhang, Hui-Min Zhao, Yan-Kui Bai

item.title: A Solar Optical Clock
item.description: arXiv:2610.28485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Connor Fredrick, Ryan K. Cole, Ryan Terrien, Suvrath Mahadevan, Scott A. Diddams

item.title: Photonic band structure by direct second-kind free-space boundary integral equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.28494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a direct boundary integral equation (BIE) formulation of the Bloch eigenvalue problem for two-dimensional photonic crystals that uses only the free-space Helmholtz Green function. The unknowns are the Cauchy data of the Bloch mode on the inclusion boundary and on two cell walls. On the inclusion boundary, the transmission conditions are imposed via M\"uller's formulation. The wall equations, in turn, come from a stack formulation, in which Green's formula is applied on stacks of three cells, so that the wall self-interactions and the interactions between arcs sharing endpoints cancel exactly. The resulting system is of the second kind, Fredholm of index zero, and free of corner singularities, and the walls may be curved to keep the cell boundary away from the inclusions. Its operators are assembled once per frequency and reused for all Bloch vectors. We prove that every Bloch mode yields a nonzero null vector, and that a null vector comes from a Bloch mode exactly when its cell representation vanishes outside the cell, which gives an inexpensive test for spurious null vectors. The band frequencies are computed with a high-order Nystr\"om discretization and the search of Bruno, Santana and Trefethen, which locates them as poles of adaptive Antoulas--Anderson (AAA) rational approximants to a randomly scalarized resolvent sampled on the real frequency axis. Numerical examples validate the method against exact and published band structures and include a challenging triangular lattice of air pores in a dielectric, whose cell requires curved walls.
item.dc:creator: Carlos P\'erez-Arancibia, Tao Yin

item.title: Diffractive neural networks for mode-sorting with flexible detection regions
item.description: arXiv:2508.20058v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mode-sorting is a procedure that decomposes a light field into a basis of transverse modes, directing each mode into a separate spatial location, allowing the constituent mode intensities to be measured simultaneously. We demonstrate a mode-sorter based on a diffractive optical neural network and show that it is advantageous to include the output detection regions into the trainable set of parameters of that network. This approach outperforms traditional mode-sorting methods, achieving lower crosstalk levels for the same efficiency. For example, in sorting 25 Hermite-Gaussian modes with a 3 plate sorter, at 12 % efficiency, the experimentally measured crosstalk decreases from 37.5 % for fixed detection to 8.7 % for flexible detection.
item.dc:creator: Kaden Bearne, Alexander Duplinskiy, Matthew J. Filipovich, A. I. Lvovsky

item.title: Widely tunable SNAP microresonators induced at the optical fiber intersections
item.description: arXiv:2604.06960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A widely tunable free spectral range (FSR) is essential for many microresonator applications, but achieving it in compact high-Q systems remains a significant challenge. Surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) provides a route to such devices by localizing whispering-gallery modes through nanoscale effective-radius variations along an optical fiber. Recently, it has been experimentally demonstrated that side-coupling between two optical fibers can induce high-Q SNAP microresonators. In contrast to broadly explored monolithic microresonators, this configuration enables extensive mechanical tuning of the microresonator configuration and FSR through fiber bending, tilting, and twisting. Here, we develop the theory of SNAP microresonators induced at optical fiber intersections, which has remained largely unexplored. We consider weakly twisted fibers, whose geometry can be decomposed into tilting and bending. We show that extremely small fiber curvature critically affects the coupling-induced cutoff frequency variation, the shape of the effective axial potential, and the spectrum of the induced resonator. We discuss the physical origin of this curvature and show that accounting for it resolves the discrepancy between theory and experiment. These findings establish side-coupled optical fibers as a simple, reconfigurable platform for realizing microresonators with a widely tunable FSR.
item.dc:creator: M. Sumetsky

item.title: Memory in Integrated Photonic Neural Networks: From Physical Mechanisms to Neuromorphic Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2604.22620v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid scaling of artificial neural networks has exposed fundamental limitations of conventional von Neumann computing architectures. In these systems, the physical separation between memory and processing creates a bottleneck, as computational capabilities outpace the ability of memory and interconnects to supply and retrieve data. In contrast, biological neural systems inherently co-localize computation and memory through distributed, dynamical processes. Neuromorphic computing seeks to emulate this paradigm by leveraging physical substrates whose intrinsic dynamics simultaneously encode and process information. Among emerging platforms, silicon photonics offers a compelling approach due to its high bandwidth, low-loss propagation, and inherent parallelism. This review examines the role of memory in integrated photonic neuromorphic systems, with emphasis on the physical mechanisms that provide volatile and non-volatile memory mechanisms, while distinguishing their retention properties from their temporal behaviour and computational role as state or parameter memory in silicon-on-insulator and hybrid silicon-on-insulator platforms. Drawing inspiration from digital, biological, and photonic memory architectures, we classify existing approaches based on their underlying physical principles. We cover implementations ranging from delay lines and slow-light structures to multistable dynamics and structural memory based on charge trapping and phase-change materials. We then discuss how these mechanisms support photonic neural network architectures, and assess their relevance for time-dependent signal-processing tasks such as channel equalization in telecommunications. This review aims to establish a unified framework for understanding memory and learning in neuromorphic photonics and outlines key challenges and opportunities for scalable, energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Foradori, Ilya Auslender, Stefano Biasi, Stefano Gretter, Alessio Lugnan, Emiliano Staffoli, Lorenzo Pavesi

item.title: Scaling Limits of Multichannel Spectral Routers for Snapshot Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2607.23508v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse-designed spectral routers can enable compact snapshot spectral imaging by directing different wavelengths to designated detector sub-pixels without mechanical scanning or absorptive filters. Here, we examine how routing performance varies as the number of spectral channels increases while the visible bandwidth remains fixed. A delay-bandwidth analysis relates channel count, worst-channel efficiency, and device thickness, explaining the growing optical capacity required to generate many spatially distinct spectral outputs. We then use adjoint-based topology optimization and three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations to design TiO2/SiO2 routers with 9, 16, 25, and 36 channels under matched material, bandwidth, and thickness conditions. The average routing efficiency increases with sub-pixel size and approaches a plateau, while the maximum near-plateau efficiency decreases monotonically from 97.0% for 9 channels to 82.3% for 36 channels. At a fixed channel count, compressing the wavelength spacing to 8 nm or rearranging the wavelength-to-sub-pixel assignment changes the efficiency by less than one percentage point. These results indicate that the observed efficiency penalty is governed mainly by the number of wavelength-dependent routing constraints rather than by wavelength spacing or local wavelength arrangement. The findings quantify the trade-off between spectral sampling and optical throughput in compact snapshot spectral imagers.
item.dc:creator: Junseo Han, Seunghyun Lee, Donghyun Kim, Haejun Chung

item.title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions in SSBM and Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method for SSBM that Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
item.description: arXiv:2608.12545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In our previous work, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a physics-based simulator for combinatorial optimization problems (SSBM), which exploits a distinctive spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) phenomenon identified in a dissipative system exhibiting robust causality described by an iterative equation. We further conducted numerical simulations in which initial fluctuations of distinct patterns were applied to large-scale benchmark problems, and reported that the SSBM exhibits a unique behavior absent in conventional Ising machines: under specific conditions, pseudo-spin patterns progressively converge during the solution-search process and ultimately coalesce into a single pattern, with the cut value of the converged solution reaching 99.7% of the best-known cut value. In the present paper, we elucidate the conditions under which the SSBM can be configured to emulate the behavior of a continuous-variable Ising machine. We further demonstrate that by additionally incorporating an effect analogous to physical annealing into these conditions, the SSBM becomes capable of identifying the best-known cut value for the K_2000 benchmark instance.
item.dc:creator: Toshiya Sato

item.title: Mechanical quality factor estimation from a nonlinear optical cavity response
item.description: arXiv:2609.07393v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intrinsic damping rate and quality factor ($Q$) are key parameters in optomechanical systems. However, in high-Q devices, their measurement is often challenging because probe-induced dynamical backaction (DBA) and the need to resolve and accurately track the mechanical resonance limit the performance of state-of-the-art techniques. Here, we introduce an all-optical ringdown method in the unresolved-sideband regime that exploits the nonlinear, time-averaged optical response induced by strong mechanical motion. We derive an analytical model of the time-averaged optical cavity response probed by a weak frequency-scanning laser. During the evolution of the mechanical oscillator, the excited motion modulates the Lorentzian lineshape into a double-horned profile whose peak separation enables an accurate estimation of the modulation amplitude. Tracking this response during the mechanical ringdown allows the intrinsic damping rate to be determined without resolving the mechanical oscillation. We apply the method to a density-modulated phononic crystal membrane placed inside a high-finesse cavity and obtain mechanical quality factors consistent with independent measurements on the same platform. Our method requires a minimal optical setup, while offering an in situ diagnostic and reduced impact from probe-induced DBA and robustness against measurement noise. Finally, the model can describe other resonant systems dispersively coupled to coherent frequency modulations, providing new insights and measurement strategies that expand beyond the optomechanical platform.
item.dc:creator: Zohran Ali, Davide Tomasella, Daniel Allepuz-Requena, Alexander Huck, Ulrik Lund Andersen

item.title: A unified sensitivity kernel for coherent wave tomography in radar, seismic, ultrasound, and optical imaging
item.description: arXiv:2609.31583v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Imaging an inhomogeneous medium with waves rests on the response of a boundary measurement to a change of the medium inside, formally the sensitivity kernel of the inverse problem. Here we show that the kernels of radar, seismology, medical ultrasound, and diffuse optics all reduce to just two classes. Every kernel is the product of a forward and an adjoint field, and a real measurement retains one quadrature of that product. These quadratures are the two classes, selected either by a component of the material parameter or by the misfit, the structure that persists for the coherent-wave kernel in both the ballistic and the diffusive regime. We place these areas on one diagram of scattering strength and transport depth, exposing a shared computational limit set by wavefield storage, and propose a broadband on-shell compression that can relax that limit.
item.dc:creator: Alexey Yamilov

item.title: Calibration-Free Photonic Memory in a Silicon Photonics Platform
item.description: arXiv:2610.00748v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a calibration-free photonic memory bitcell based on nonresonant variable optical attenuators in the GlobalFoundries 45SPCLO platform. The cell maintains complementary electrical states through electro-optical feedback without cavity-resonance alignment. Wordline-controlled attenuators enable selective writing through differential optical bitlines, while optical readout shares the holding input and output splitters, avoiding additional read attenuators or a separate laser source. Circuit simulations demonstrate writing with $10~\mathrm{ps}$ optical pulses at $2~\mathrm{mW}$ peak power. The cell retains data as long as optical and electrical power are supplied, with retention simulated for $5~\mathrm{s}$ per logic state. The evaluated transition consumes an incremental write energy of $0.562~\mathrm{pJ}$, including circuit electrical energy and the laser contribution at 20\% wall-plug efficiency. The bitcell layout occupies $147.92\times219.93~\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}$.
item.dc:creator: Ankur Singh, Akhilesh Jaiswal

item.title: Projection-based coupling of infrared thermography and stereocorrelation-based digital image correlation
item.description: arXiv:2606.28905v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Full-field measurement techniques such as digital image correlation and infrared thermography are prevalent in experimental solid mechanics. Digital image correlation is used to analyze surface deformation, while infrared thermography quantifies surface temperature fields. However, sophisticated procedures are necessary to express both datasets in the same Lagrangian frame, especially when analyzing non-flat surfaces. In this study, we propose an external projection-based coupling that uses the pinhole camera model to relate two-dimensional temperature data measured by infrared thermography to three-dimensional point coordinates from stereocorrelation-based digital image correlation. Unlike existing multiview approaches, we utilize two independently calibrated industrial-grade systems and augment the experimental evaluation with the pinhole camera model. The projection matrix of the camera model is calibrated using a single image of a reference object. Through this projection, temperature fields are accurately represented at material points. Our method is particularly suited for, but not restricted to, curved surfaces and is straightforward to embed in existing experimental protocols, as the image registration is kept as is. Additionally, we use radial basis functions as a global interpolation ansatz in both space and time to compute in-plane temperature gradients and even temperature rates on curved surfaces, thereby providing an extensive and information-rich full-field dataset.
item.dc:creator: Jendrik-Alexander Tr\"oger, Lutz M\"uller-Lohse, Stefan Hartmann

item.title: A semiconductor photon-pair source based on a polariton cascade
item.description: arXiv:2609.17900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a theoretical study of a semiconductor photon-pair source based on a radiative cascade enabled by a permanent exciton dipole. The source consists of a GaAs quantum dot placed between a metal nanoparticle and a mirror. The dot exciton and the localized electromagnetic mode mix to form upper and lower polaritons. Without a permanent dipole, a symmetry separating states with even and odd excitation numbers forbids photon emission between the polaritons. Separation of the mean electron and hole positions gives the exciton a permanent dipole and breaks this symmetry. The upper polariton can then emit an idler photon as it decays to the lower polariton. The lower polariton can emit a signal photon as the system returns to its ground state. Using an effective model, we calculate the probability that a prepared upper polariton emits both photons through the metal antenna. We also analyze fluctuations in the emitted photon counts and correlations between the two emission channels. The calculation establishes an operating principle for assumed values of the coupling strength, emitter properties and optical loss rates. Whether the device can be built and its photon correlations measured remains open.
item.dc:creator: Karol Kawa
